title: Ensemble structure and double clarinets
summary: They play the melody once, then solos, then two final choruses; sometimes two clarinets, as Kid Rene's band did. Few bands still use banjo.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: Let me see now. How many choruses of ensemble do you all usually play at the beginning of a tune?
Oh, you're gonna have to break that down for me now.
I mean, would you, uh, would you play, go through the melody once or twice?

Well, uh, usually once, huh? That's, uh, yeah, we'll go through it. Most of the time once. Most of the time once, then, uh, each, uh, instrument will take his solo. Then, uh, we'll take two choruses at the end, see, knock it out in two choruses.
Sometimes you play pairs, don't you?
Yeah, I will sometimes, uh, uh, maybe a...

A clarinet and the, uh, the trombone might, uh, take half, each one will take half a chorus. Maybe the piano and the banjo might take half and half. You know, something like that. Well, they might play it together. They might play it together. Well, uh, you have to...
I've got some pretty good, uh, two clarinet stuff up there.

Well, we use a double clarinet. We, uh, uh, well, uh, Bill, Bill Lee has been, uh, doubling with his, uh, soprano and his clarinet and his alto. And, uh, sometimes he and, uh, Briss will take a clarinet, uh, duet, you know. And it's, uh, I think, uh, Alphonse Pico and, uh, Big Eye, Louis Nelson, used to play that way. On a couple of recordings, they used a double clarinet. With Kid René.

Yeah, that's an old time thing. All the guys, tell me they used to do that. I've heard Emile Barnes and, uh, Albert Burbank together. They didn't have a trumpet play at one time, you know. And I sat in on the trombone. Yeah. And it was fun, you know, to hear them play like that. It sounded good. And John Handy and Willie Humphrey used to do that, too. Yeah.

Well, I don't think, uh, you'll see too many of the bands around the city now that do anything like that. No. I mean, it's just a novelty with us. Another thing, you hardly will see a banjo in your bands anymore. You see, or a toolbar, as far as that goes. You don't see things like that anymore. So I think that's what we are more or less capitalizing on, is the fact that we are reproducing the old, the real old sound, see. And, uh, that's what's keeping us going.
